Simon M. Smith, Group Theory pg.27 4.3 Consequences and applications of Lagrange’s Theorem Corollary 4.3.1. Let H be a subgroup of a finite group G, and suppose g ∈ G. Then (i) [G ∶ H] = ∣G∣/∣H∣ (ii) o(g) divides ∣G∣ Proof. The proof of (i) is easy: by Lagrange, ∣G∣ = [G ∶ H] ⋅ ∣H∣, therefore ∣G∣/∣H∣ = [G ∶ H]. To prove (ii), let H = ⟨g⟩. By Proposition 2.3.2 we know that o(g) = ∣⟨g⟩∣ = ∣H∣. By Lagrange, ∣H∣ = o(g) divides the order of G. Example 4.3.2. Here are two example applications of Lagrange’s Theorem that are basically the same. 1. The Dihedral group D10 does not contain an element of order 7. Proof: ∣D10∣ = 10 = 2 ⋅ 5. If D10 contained an element of order 7, then 7 would divide 10 which it does not. 2. The Dihedral group D10 does not contain a subgroup of order 7. Proof: if it did, then again 7∣10 which is false. ! Warning! The converse statement to Lagrange’s Theorem does not hold—just because a number divides ∣G∣, this does not mean that G has a subgroup of that order (the smallest couterexample has order 12 and is called the Alternating Group of degree 4. We will see this group later in the course). Application of Lagrange’s Theorem: how to understand the dihedral group Recall D2n = {e, ρ, . . . , ρ n−1, σ1, . . . , σn} where the σi are reflections and ρ is the cycle (1 2 . . . n). Can we do better with the reflections? First, notice that ∣D2n∣ = 2n. Let C = ⟨ρ⟩ = {e, ρ, . . . , ρn−1}. Notice that ∣C∣ = n and C ≤ D2n. By Lagrange’s Theorem: ∣D2n∣ = [D2n ∶ C] ⋅ ∣C∣ Where [D2n ∶ C] is the number of cosets of C in D2n. Hence, [D2n ∶ C] = ∣D2n∣ ∣C∣ = 2n n = 2. Let σ = σ1. Since σ /∈ C, we know (from Theorem 4.1.3) that C /= σC, and so the two cosets of C in D2n must be C and σC. Hence D2n = C ∪ σC. The reflections don’t lie in C, so they must all lie in σC. This means that all the reflections are of the form σρ i. Thus, D2n = {e, ρ, ρ 2, . . . , ρn−1, σ, σρ, σρ2, . . . , σρn−1}. This is great, but we have a problem: how do we calculate things like ρσ? It’s not in the above list of elements in D2n. What about even more complicated things, like ρσρσρ 2σ? We start with ρσ. It is easy to see that ρσ is not a translation (it reverses the label order on the corners), so it must be a reflection and therefore has order 2. Hence (ρσ)(ρσ) = e. Therefore, ρσ = (ρσ)−1 = σ−1ρ−1 = σρ −1 = σρ n−1. We can use this trick to calculate: ρ 2σ, ρ3σ, . . . , ρn−1σ. Important summary: D2n = {e, ρ, ρ2, . . . , ρn−1, σ, σρ, σρ2, . . . , σρn−1}, with ρσ = σρ −1 and ρn = e and σ2 = e. We can use the important summary above to easily work out combinations of rotations and reflections. Question 4.3.3. Which element of D2n = {e, ρ, ρ 2, . . . , ρn−1, σ, σρ, σρ2, . . . , σρn−1} are the following equal to? 1. ρ3σ (Answer: ρ 3σ = ρ2σρ −1 = ρσρ −2 = σρ −3 = σρ n−3) 2. ρσρσρ2σ (Answer: ρσρσρ 2σ = σρ−1ρσρ 2σ = σσρ2σ = ρ2σ = ρσρ−1 = σρ −2 = σρ n−2) Remark 4.3.4. What does σ look like in cycle notation? If σ is the line of reflection through the corner labelled 1, then as a permutation it is: σ = (2 n)(3 n − 1)(4 n − 2)⋯
